notes:
THE DEATH AND RESURRECTION OF JESUS - STUDY NOTES

Note: the topic is also looked at in Section H (The Bible: Literature and Sacred Text), Section C (World Religions) and Section A (The Search for Meaning and Values). The chapter shows two paintings: ‘The Taking of Christ’ by Caravaggio and ‘The Resurrection’ by Teniers the Younger.

OPENING QUOTE (JOHN 19:16-18)
- ‘So they took Jesus; and carrying the cross by himself, he went out to what is called The Place of the Skull, which in Hebrew is called Golgotha. There they crucified him.’

KEY TERMS
- New covenant: the new agreement between the people and God, in which Jesus offered himself (at the Last Supper / Passover meal).
- Crucifixion: a distinctly Roman method of execution - the most humiliating and cruel punishment, used for the lowest criminals.
- Resurrection: Jesus rising from the dead; he passed through death and was changed but still recognisable. Belief in it is a statement of faith.
- Images and metaphors: ways of describing Jesus that grew up in the early years of the Church as followers came to understand who he was.
- Incarnation: God’s revelation in the person of Jesus of Nazareth (‘the mystery of the Incarnation’).
- Mission: the task given to the disciples to carry on the work begun in Jesus (Matthew 28:19).
- Community: the new shared life of Jesus’ followers after the Resurrection (Acts 2:42-47).
- Ransom: the price paid for freedom. Jesus paid the ‘ransom’ for our freedom from sin and death.
- Redemption / redeem: to buy something back or pay for it. Comes from slavery - a slave could be redeemed if someone bought their freedom.
- Acronym: a word made from the first letters of other words. The five Greek letters of ‘fish’ stand for ‘Jesus Christ, Son of God, Saviour’.
- Mediator of salvation: Jesus as the one through whom all people are reconciled to God.

PART 1: THE ARREST OF JESUS

THE FINAL VISIT TO JERUSALEM
- After three years travelling the countryside, Jesus made his final visit to Jerusalem.
- This put him in danger: he came into the jurisdiction (area of power) of those he had fundamentally challenged.
- He must have been aware of the possible consequences.
- By coming to Jerusalem he was challenging both the Roman authorities and the Jewish authorities.
- His friend John the Baptist had already been killed because of his teaching.
- By the time Jesus entered Jerusalem, his large band of followers had probably dwindled to the most loyal, as people were afraid and nervous.

CLEARING THE TEMPLE
- Jesus cleared the Temple of those who used it for personal economic gain.
- In doing this he was calling for the renewal of the covenant between Yahweh and the people of God.
- Part of this renewal was restoring the Temple as a place where the covenant was honoured.
- The Jewish religious leaders closely linked with the Temple saw this as a threat.

THE LAST NIGHT: PASSOVER WITH HIS FOLLOWERS
- On the night before he died, before his arrest, Jesus celebrated Passover with his followers.
- Symbolic act of service: he washed the feet of his disciples and asked that they too would do this in his memory.
- He shared a meal with his friends and spoke of the sacrifice he was preparing to make.
- By this time Jesus knew he faced death.
- He asked his disciples to remember him in word and deed.
- He prepared them for what lay ahead (probably only clear to them after he died).
- Jesus offered himself in a NEW COVENANT between the people and God.

ARREST AND TRIAL
- Jesus was arrested, put on trial and condemned to death in Jerusalem.
- There is some disagreement about the exact charge.
- He appeared before the Jewish leaders (the SANHEDRIN) and the Roman authorities (PONTIUS PILATE).
- Depending on their audience, each gospel writer underplayed or highlighted the part played by the Jewish authorities.
- The arrest, trial and execution is the high point of all four gospels - a dramatic and shocking end. Each gospel covers it in great detail.

THE MOST CERTAIN FACT ABOUT JESUS (QUOTED PASSAGE)
- The most certain and well-attested fact about Jesus is that he was tried, sentenced and executed by the Roman procurator Pontius Pilate on a charge of high treason.
- This did not make him unique: many thousands of Jewish rebels and revolutionaries were crucified by the Romans in Palestine at this time.
- Jews on the whole opposed Roman rule; some wanted to overthrow the Romans and restore the kingdom of Israel.
- Jesus was found guilty of being involved in some such conspiracy, and of claiming to be the rightful king of the Jews, heir to the throne - what the Jews would call the Messiah.
- The inscription above his cross (‘The King of the Jews’) leaves no doubt about the charge.

THE CHARGE: BLASPHEMY OR TREASON?
- Jesus seems to have been charged with either blasphemy or treason.
- He was accused of claiming to be the Son of God, the Messiah.
- This was NOT a capital offence (deserving death) within Judaism, even if the charge was accurate.
- The chapter says Jesus himself never claimed the titles ‘Son of God’ or ‘Messiah’. Rather, many who heard and saw him regarded him as such and proclaimed him their messiah and saviour.
- Many believed he had come to rescue them from Roman occupation and would lead a revolution.
- Others saw him as the Messiah promised in their scriptures who would lead them into a new age.
- So the Romans may have been nervous of this rabbi from Galilee stirring up nationalist fervour among the Jews.
- All four gospels mention a sign or placard reading ‘The King of the Jews’.
- Mark 15:26: ‘The inscription of the charge against him read, “The King of the Jews”.’
- This suggests Jesus was put to death because of the threat he posed to the Roman Empire.
- Other possibility: he was charged with threatening the destruction of the Temple. Any challenge to the religion could be seen as an attack on the Temple. In Judaism this would be treason.

TWO FACTS NOT DISPUTED
- Scholars may disagree about whether Jesus was tried before the Sanhedrin, or the exact offence. But they agree:
- 1. Jesus was sentenced to death by Pontius Pilate.
- 2. Jesus was crucified.

CRUCIFIXION
- A distinctly Roman method of execution.
- Flogging or ‘scourging’ traditionally came before crucifixion - Jesus was no exception.
- Like others, he carried his own cross to the place of execution - the hill of Calvary (Golgotha, ‘The Place of the Skull’).
- He suffered a slow and painful death.
- Historians of the time show crucifixion was the most humiliating and cruel punishment of all, used for the lowest criminals.
- Jesus was almost certainly stripped and nailed to the cross.
- The pain of this deliberately slow, brutal death is hardly imaginable today.

PART 2: THE RESURRECTION

AFTER THE CROSS
- The story of Jesus did not end at the cross. Something extraordinary happened after his death.
- It is recorded in the gospel accounts of his appearances and of what became of his small band of followers.
- His death was deeply shocking for his followers. They were left without their leader.
- Some ran away in terror; some may have lost hope and gone home; others wondered what it was all about and what to do now.
- Jesus had told them they would face hard times and their faith would be tested, and that he would be with them always - and now he was gone.
- The Resurrection must be understood in this context.

THE EMPTY TOMB
- There were NO witnesses to the resurrection itself.
- When Mary Magdalene found no body in the tomb, her first thought was that it had been stolen.
- John 20:2: ‘They have taken the Lord out of the tomb, and we do not know where they have laid him.’
- The gospels tell of a tomb with only ‘linen wrappings’ (John 20:6).

THE APPEARANCES
- Jesus appeared in a changed but recognisable form.
- He had changed because he had passed through death, but those who saw him still recognised him when he spoke to them.
- This ‘change’ is part of the mystery of Jesus Christ. Jesus defeated death.
- The appearances and the empty tomb are the ‘evidence’ of the resurrection.
- But belief in the resurrection cannot be based only on historical evidence. Belief in the Resurrection is a STATEMENT OF FAITH.

APPEARANCE TO MARY MAGDALENE (JOHN 20:13-16)
- She is asked, ‘Woman, why are you weeping?’ She says, ‘They have taken away my Lord, and I do not know where they have laid him.’
- She turns and sees Jesus but does not know it is him.
- Jesus asks, ‘Woman, why are you weeping? For whom are you looking?’
- Thinking he is the gardener, she asks where he has laid the body.
- Jesus says, ‘Mary!’ She turns and says in Hebrew, ‘Rabbouni!’ (which means Teacher).

PAUL’S ACCOUNT (1 CORINTHIANS 15:3-8)
- One of the most significant accounts.
- Paul hands on what he received ‘as of first importance’: Christ died for our sins in accordance with the scriptures; he was buried; he was raised on the third day in accordance with the scriptures.
- Order of appearances: to Cephas (Peter); then to the twelve; then to more than five hundred brothers and sisters at one time (most still alive); then to James; then to all the apostles; last of all to Paul himself, ‘as to someone untimely born’.
- Effects of the appearances:
- the disciples were reassured and given instructions on how to carry on
- they were reminded of their mission and focus
- they were transformed and moved to act together to continue Jesus’ work.

ROAD TO EMMAUS (GROUP WORK)
- Luke 24:13-35 - Cleopas and his friend meet the risen Jesus on the road to Emmaus. Students are asked when they recognised him and what effect the meeting had.
- The four gospel Resurrection accounts to compare: Matthew 28:1-15; Mark 16:1-13; Luke 24:1-49; John 20:1-21, 24-28 (compare the description, the appearances, and people’s reactions).

PART 3: THE FIRST CHRISTIANS STRUGGLE TO UNDERSTAND THE CALVARY EVENT
- Only after the death and resurrection did Jesus’ followers begin to understand who he was.
- The resurrection and appearances forced them to see Jesus was more than they had imagined.
- Many images and metaphors of Jesus come from these early years of the emerging Church.
- God had been revealed through Jesus. Jesus was a high point in the history of God’s self-revelation.
- God’s revelation in the person of Jesus of Nazareth is called the mystery of the INCARNATION.
- John 14:9: ‘Whoever has seen me has seen the Father.’
- Colossians 1:15: ‘He is the image of the invisible God.’

THE SENSE OF MISSION
- Matthew 28:19: ‘Go, therefore, and make disciples of all nations, baptising them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, and teaching them to obey everything that I have commanded you. And remember, I am with you always, to the end of the age.’
- Jesus was again present among his people - they were no longer alone.
- His words and deeds took on new significance in the light of the Resurrection.
- There was a dramatic change in the disciples after the experience of the Spirit (promised by Jesus) at PENTECOST.
- They knew they had a mission to carry on Jesus’ work and that he would be with them always.

AWARENESS OF COMMUNITY (ACTS 2:42-47)
- The followers had a new awareness of community after the Resurrection.
- ‘They devoted themselves to the apostles’ teaching and fellowship, to the breaking of bread and the prayers.’
- Awe came upon everyone because of many wonders and signs done by the apostles.
- All who believed were together and had all things in common.
- They sold possessions and goods and distributed the proceeds to all, as any had need.
- Day by day they spent time together in the temple, broke bread at home and ate with glad and generous hearts.
- They praised God and had the goodwill of all the people.
- Day by day the Lord added to their number those being saved.

PART 4: JESUS AS THE MEDIATOR OF SALVATION
- As well as revealing God, Jesus was understood as Saviour - not only of his followers, but of all God’s people.
- Jesus paid the ultimate price for humanity: the ‘ransom’ for our freedom from sin and death.
- Evidence of this early belief: the FISH as an early Christian symbol. The five Greek letters spelling ‘fish’ are an acronym of ‘Jesus Christ, Son of God, Saviour’.
- RANSOM and REDEMPTION are related terms. To redeem is to buy back or pay for something.
- The terms probably came from slavery: a slave could be redeemed if someone bought their freedom.
- Early Christians understood Jesus as having redeemed all humanity.
- He was the means of reconciliation between God and humanity.
- Through Jesus all people became reconciled to God, who loved them so much that he sent his Son to be their Saviour.
- Jesus was the MEDIATOR OF SALVATION.

TEXTBOOK QUESTIONS, ASSIGNMENTS AND REFLECTIONS
- What was the new covenant Jesus offered? What charge was laid against Jesus? Describe crucifixion at the time of Jesus.
- Diary of a disciple who saw the arrest and trial; letter home from a Roman soldier; a time you felt alone and afraid.
- Reflection: read the trial and execution in a gospel; follow the Way of the Cross / Stations of the Cross.
- Reflection: imagine you were a follower at the cross; what are the signs of Christ’s presence today? (see chapter two).
- Essay: trace the events of Calvary from arrest to resurrection - historical events and religious significance.
- Note on the new awareness of community after the Resurrection, and how it might differ from the Church today.

rows.prompt: Why was Jesus placing himself in danger by going to Jerusalem?
rows.model_answer: Jerusalem was under the power of those he had fundamentally challenged, both Roman and Jewish authorities. His friend John the Baptist had already been killed for his teaching. When he cleared the Temple of those using it for economic gain, the religious leaders linked to the Temple saw him as a threat.

rows.prompt: Describe what Jesus did at the Passover meal on the night before he died.
rows.model_answer: He washed his disciples’ feet as a symbolic act of service and asked them to do the same in his memory. He shared a meal and spoke of the sacrifice he was about to make, asked them to remember him in word and deed, and offered himself in a new covenant between the people and God.

rows.prompt: Explain the two possible charges against Jesus.
rows.model_answer: He may have been charged with blasphemy or treason. He was accused of claiming to be the Son of God, the Messiah, and the sign ‘The King of the Jews’ (Mark 15:26) suggests he was killed as a threat to the Roman Empire. Another possibility is that he was charged with threatening the destruction of the Temple, which in Judaism would be treason.

rows.prompt: Describe crucifixion as a method of execution at the time of Jesus.
rows.model_answer: Crucifixion was a distinctly Roman punishment, the most humiliating and cruel of all, used for the lowest criminals. It was usually preceded by flogging or scourging. The condemned carried their own cross to the place of execution; Jesus was stripped and nailed to the cross on Calvary and suffered a deliberately slow, painful death.

rows.prompt: What is the ‘evidence’ for the Resurrection, and why is belief in it a statement of faith?
rows.model_answer: The evidence is the empty tomb, with only linen wrappings left, and the appearances of Jesus in a changed but recognisable form. There were no witnesses to the resurrection itself. So belief cannot rest only on historical evidence; it is a statement of faith.

rows.prompt: According to 1 Corinthians 15:3-8, to whom did the risen Jesus appear?
rows.model_answer: He appeared to Cephas, then to the twelve, then to more than five hundred brothers and sisters at one time, then to James, then to all the apostles, and last of all to Paul himself.

rows.prompt: Describe the new awareness of community among the first Christians (Acts 2:42-47).
rows.model_answer: They devoted themselves to the apostles’ teaching and fellowship, the breaking of bread and the prayers. They held all things in common, sold their goods and shared with anyone in need, met in the temple and broke bread at home with glad and generous hearts. The Lord added to their number day by day.

rows.prompt: Explain what is meant by calling Jesus the ‘mediator of salvation’, using the terms ransom and redemption.
rows.model_answer: Jesus paid the ultimate price, the ‘ransom’, for humanity’s freedom from sin and death. To redeem is to buy back, as when a slave’s freedom was bought. Early Christians believed Jesus redeemed all humanity and reconciled people to God, who loved them enough to send his Son as Saviour.

rows.prompt: Write an essay tracing the events of Calvary from the arrest of Jesus to his resurrection, referring to both the historical events and their religious significance.
rows.model_answer: After three years of travelling, Jesus came to Jerusalem, into the power of those he had challenged. He cleared the Temple, calling for renewal of the covenant, which the Temple leaders saw as a threat. On the night before he died he celebrated Passover, washed his disciples’ feet as an act of service and offered himself in a new covenant between the people and God. He was arrested and appeared before the Sanhedrin and the Roman procurator Pontius Pilate. The exact charge is debated: blasphemy, treason, or threatening the Temple. The sign ‘The King of the Jews’ (Mark 15:26) suggests he was seen as a threat to Rome. Scholars agree he was sentenced by Pilate and crucified. He was scourged, carried his cross to Calvary, and was stripped and nailed to the cross, the most humiliating Roman punishment. His followers were shocked; some fled. But Mary Magdalene found the tomb empty, with only linen wrappings, and Jesus appeared to her, calling her by name. Paul (1 Corinthians 15:3-8) lists appearances to Cephas, the twelve, over five hundred, James and himself. Religiously, the Resurrection is a statement of faith: Jesus defeated death, and his followers came to see him as the Saviour who paid the ransom for sin.
rows.marking_scheme: Very good 16-20, good 10-15, fair 0-9. Marks for historical events: final visit, Temple, Passover/foot-washing/new covenant, arrest, Sanhedrin and Pilate, charge, scourging, crucifixion, empty tomb, appearances. Marks for religious significance: new covenant, statement of faith, defeat of death, Saviour/ransom, mission. Both strands needed for very good.

rows.prompt: (a) What charge was laid against Jesus? (b) Describe crucifixion as a method of execution at the time of Jesus.
rows.model_answer:
(a) There is some disagreement about the exact charge. The most certain fact about Jesus is that he was tried, sentenced and executed by the Roman procurator Pontius Pilate on a charge of high treason. He was accused of claiming to be the Son of God, the Messiah. This was not a capital offence in Judaism, but the Romans may have been nervous of a Galilean rabbi stirring up nationalist fervour, since many hoped he would lead a revolution against Rome. All four gospels mention a sign reading ‘The King of the Jews’ (Mark 15:26), which suggests he was killed as a threat to the Empire. Another possibility is that he was charged with threatening the destruction of the Temple, which in Judaism would be treason.
(b) Crucifixion was a distinctly Roman method of execution, the most humiliating and cruel punishment, used for the lowest criminals. It was usually preceded by flogging or scourging. The condemned man carried his own cross to the place of execution; Jesus carried his to the hill of Calvary. He was stripped and nailed to the cross and suffered a deliberately slow, brutal and painful death.
rows.marking_scheme: (a) 10 marks: very good 8-10, good 5-7, fair 0-4. May refer to: high treason; Pilate; claim to be Messiah/king; not capital in Judaism; ‘The King of the Jews’ Mark 15:26; threat to Temple; thousands of rebels crucified. (b) 10 marks: Roman; scourging; carrying cross; Calvary; stripped and nailed; slow painful death; humiliating, for lowest criminals.

rows.prompt: Explain how the Resurrection changed the followers of Jesus.
rows.model_answer: The death of Jesus was deeply shocking for his followers. They were left without their leader; some ran away in terror, some lost hope and went home, and others wondered what to do next. After the Resurrection, Jesus appeared to them in a changed but recognisable form. Through these appearances they were reassured, given instructions on how to carry on and reminded of their mission, and they were moved to act together to continue his work. They began to understand who Jesus really was: God revealed in him (‘Whoever has seen me has seen the Father’, John 14:9). They received a sense of mission (‘make disciples of all nations’, Matthew 28:19) and after Pentecost they changed dramatically. They also formed a community that shared everything (Acts 2:42-47).
rows.marking_scheme: Before (shock, fear, loss of hope) 2 marks. After: reassured and instructed, mission (Matthew 28:19), understanding of who Jesus was / Incarnation, Pentecost, community (Acts 2:42-47) - 2 marks each up to 8.

rows.prompt: Discuss how the first Christians came to understand Jesus as the Saviour and mediator of salvation.
rows.model_answer: Only after the death and resurrection did Jesus’ followers begin to understand who he was. The Resurrection forced them to see that he was more than they had imagined, and many images and metaphors of Jesus come from these early years. They saw that God had been revealed in Jesus, a high point in God’s self-revelation known as the mystery of the Incarnation (John 14:9, Colossians 1:15). They also understood Jesus as Saviour, not only of his followers but of all God’s people. Jesus paid the ultimate price for humanity, the ‘ransom’ for our freedom from sin and death. Ransom and redemption are related terms: to redeem is to buy back, as when someone bought a slave’s freedom. The early Christians believed Jesus had redeemed all humanity and reconciled people to God, who loved them so much that he sent his Son to be their Saviour. The fish symbol supports this: the five Greek letters of ‘fish’ are an acronym of ‘Jesus Christ, Son of God, Saviour’. In this way Jesus was the mediator of salvation.
